title: Zen and Two Worlds
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads aloud a draft of his article "Zen and Two Worlds" for The Sun, a travelogue of a summer trip to Japan with his wife Cathy. A mossy temple garden in Fuji-Kawaguchiko, a Japanese tourist office in San Francisco, and a nun giving an old woman a back massage at Toji soften his long-held antipathy toward Japanese Zen. A morning service at Eiheiji, with acolytes passing out sutra books like ballet dancers, shows him priests trained to mediate between the ordinary and liminal worlds. Norman then contrasts Japan's Buddhist roots with America's lack of an established religion, and wonders whether fundamentalism is a cry to return to the liminal world. He ends by asking how people of different faiths might talk peacefully about what matters most.

sentences.text: Well, as Tim said, I've been a full-time Zen student for a long time.
Actually, my entire adult life, and this has been a big surprise to me.
This was not my intention.
I began as an artist, a poet, and I still maintain my poetry practice after all this time.
But I realized early on in my career as a poet that what interested me was not recording or expressing my life.
And I wasn't all that terribly impressed by beautiful and eloquent words.
I realized that I just had questions about reality.
Somehow it seemed to me that poetry would be one way of exploring these questions.
And these were the same questions that eventually led me to study Zen, and to keep studying Zen until today.
So despite myself, I have become interested in religion.
What is religion, actually?
Why is it that everywhere in the world you find people practicing different religions?
Why is it that when you go back and dig up the ruins of some super ancient city, you find that they practice religion in every culture known to humankind?
Why is it that religion always goes wrong somehow?
Why is this the most common thing in the world?
What does religion have to do with our psychological lives?
What does religion have to do with our social lives?

And it just turned out that since I've been doing Zen practice for such a long time, and in this time when Zen is being transmitted for the first time to the West, I've had a chance to explore these questions.
And my life, in a way, you could say, has been kind of living out of many of these questions.
Sometimes, because of my unfortunate writing habit, I end up writing about these questions.
Not because I know the answers to them, but because I want to raise these questions out loud.
So this summer I was on a trip to Japan, and that gave me another place from which to view my questions.
When I came back from Japan, the editors of Sun magazine, you know that magazine, The Sun?
Yeah.
I didn't really know the magazine much, but somehow I had written some article that they published, and they emailed me and they said, would you write an article for The Sun?
And I said, OK, what if I write an article about my trip to Japan and some thoughts that I have about that?
And they said, OK.
So I sent them a copy of the article and they thought it would be a good idea to publish it.
So what I want to do tonight is actually try out this draft of this article on you and see what you think.
And you can tell me afterward if you think it makes any sense.
The title of the article is Zen and the Two Worlds.
It is a bit of a travelogue, and I hope that you'll have fun joining me in a trip to Japan.
But also partly it's some reflections on these questions that I've mentioned.
So here's the article.
*We were in Fuji-Kawaguchiko, a resort town on one of the large lakes at the foot of Mount Fuji in Japan.
It was July.
We'd come to see and even possibly climb Mount Fuji, but of course we couldn't see Mount Fuji at all, only roiling silver-gray clouds which were attractive in their own way.
We weren't disappointed.
We'd expected as much.
Japanese summers are famously humid, and so they're often also cloudy and rainy.
And Fuji's absence is nearly as famous as its presence.
Besides, I am used to the idea that the more you count on the arrival of a very important experience or accomplishment you are so much planning on, the more likely it is that it won't materialize.
And that instead you might get to enjoy something completely different.*
*Studying such normal human phenomena is one of the pleasures of Zen practice.
When I was abbot of Green Gulch Farm Zen Center in the country near San Francisco, we'd go out every year in the pre-dawn for the annual celebration of Buddha's enlightenment.
The idea was that we were going out to see the morning star, just as the Buddha had seen the morning star on the night of his awakening.
Most years we saw fog, no stars.

So I had been practicing this for many years, and so my wife Cathy and I were not too fazed by the fact that we were not, as the brochure promised, sitting in the ofuro of our hotel gazing out at Mount Fuji.
But instead we were strolling around Lake Kawaguchi under very active clouds.

The path around the lake was bordered with tall grasses and extensive plantings of gorgeous blue, pink, purple, and white hydrangeas that were much more delicate and subtle than the big garish ones you see in old-fashioned American gardens.
And though there were a fair number of resort hotels around the lake, the path this day was unpeopled.
We shared the walk only with a backpacking European couple, an old Japanese man walking his teensy white dog, and an ancient farmer tending his vegetable patch.*
*Though a resort town, Fuji-Kawaguchiko is not fancy or overdone, in fact, it's a rather ordinary, dull spot.

And we spent a lot of time walking up and down the streets whose local shops reminded me of the small town I grew up in in the days before malls and high-concept chain stores made shopping exciting rather than utilitarian.
Fuji-Kawaguchiko streets were a far cry from the glitz and glam that we'd experienced in Kyoto's downtown precincts.
One of our strolls we noticed, as one can notice almost anywhere in Japan, even on busy, wild streets, a torii gate that signaled the entrance to a small temple compound, so we went in.
Walking into the temple compound was like walking literally into another universe, a place that was quiet, serene, and felt holy.
Just beyond the gate was a small mossy garden with irregular stepping stones that led to a steadily dripping, tiny, delicate waterfall.*

*Off to one side was a standing figure of Guanyin, Bodhisattva of Compassion, on a formal lotus pedestal, looking down at us with a modest and knowing smile that carried the ancient Buddhist feeling that all would be well in the midst of a world of inevitable suffering.
The temple building, like the garden, was solid.
It was really beautiful.
It was well-kept.
And though its heavy wooden door was locked, you could walk around on the veranda or you could sit on the steps looking out into the garden.
We felt really at home here.
Everything slowed down.
We were refreshed.*
*For years I've been impatient with Japanese Buddhism's formality, aestheticism, and basic irrelevance to any sort of actual spiritual transformation.
When I began studying Zen in 1970 and reading about it some years before that, my attitude was almost the reverse of this.
In those days I was really enamored of Japanese Zen's dynamic relationship to the arts.
And I don't think I would be exaggerating to say that in Japan all the traditional arts owe their existence to Zen.
And I loved the Japanese sensibility in general and Zen's relationship to it.
And that's what appealed to me.
It was a long time ago.
I was young.
I was a poet.
I was part of a generation that was in revolt against American values.
And everything Japanese struck me as entirely superior in every way to the crude violence of the West.
But that was 1970.
All my years of Zen practice in America had changed my attitude drastically.*
*Seeing the raw and actual spiritual needs of people I was practicing with, I came to realize that flower arranging, tea sipping, and raked gravel gardening was not going to be of much help to them.

And certainly the complicated, bureaucratic, and stiflingly traditional Japanese Zen establishment that I'd come to know and have dealings with over the years was probably also not going to help them.
Meditation practice might help.
Teachings about how to work with suffering, with afflictive states of mind, might help.
Communities of support and guidance might help.
But I don't think flower arranging would help.

So between Japanese Zen's general irrelevance and also the new scholarship that was just since I guess the late 80s, early 90s, the new scholarship that was just being done that was highlighting Japanese Zen's really shameful conduct during the period before and during World War II.
With all this, I had gradually, without even necessarily realizing it, developed a fairly thoroughgoing antipathy toward Japanese Zen.*
*And this is rather an odd and troubling attitude for a senior American Zen priest and abbot in a Japanese lineage to have.
So I didn't particularly consider this a problem or even notice it or pay any attention to it until when we were getting ready to go to Japan.
By the way, it was my wife Cathy's idea to go to Japan, not my idea.
I was going because she wanted to go.
I'd been to Japan before and I had no intention of ever going back.
But she wanted to go, so I went.*

*Anyway, preparing for the trip to Japan, we went into the Japanese tourist office in San Francisco because we needed to get a Japan Rail Pass and you have to go to the Japanese tourist office to get that.
And as soon as I walked into that obscure sort of 10th floor office in a downtown building in San Francisco, it was like going to Japan.
Just walking into the Japanese tourist office, it was like going to Japan.
The place was very quiet, stacked all over with clutter like a typical Japanese office or home.
And everybody who works in the Japanese tourist office in San Francisco is Japanese, not Japanese American, but Japanese.
So as soon as you enter the space, you feel the pervasive aura of politeness and quiet courtesy that really is at the heart of the Japanese way of being.
It's possible that arrogance and aggression are also basic to the Japanese way of being.
I don't know.
But anyway, these things were not in evidence in the Japanese tourist office.
Just to walk into the Japanese tourist office in San Francisco and interact with the people there who were so wonderful and so sweet, it just melted my heart.*
*And it reminded me of how tenderly I used to feel about all things Japanese and what a warm feeling I always had whenever I would encounter Japanese people.
And I still have that feeling, actually, but I forgot about it.
And so it kind of came out when I went to the tourist office.
But you know, it occurred to me that this is what happens to every one of us.
In the ordinary course of things, we fix on something that is partly true and partly not true.
And without realizing it, we fix that notion into a prejudice.
And then prejudiced or blind to the other possibilities, unless we're lucky enough to go into the Japanese tourist office.
So in a similar way, entering that small and quite ordinary temple compound in Fuji-Kawaguchiko reminded me that actually there is more to Japanese Zen than formality, bureaucracy, and aesthetics.
We in the West have managed to take the quiet, holy, sacred world and reduce it to what we call the inner life, which can be safely crammed into the space between our ears.*
*Our scientific spirit has given us explanations that tame and disarm the uncharted world of mystery and allow us to dispense with the need for powers beyond ourselves.
Japanese society, too, is saturated with the scientific spirit.
But unlike ours, it has preserved in its atavistic layers a Buddhist religious sensibility.
However unclear that sensibility may be to most Japanese people, it nevertheless lives within and all around them.
When Japanese people enter a temple compound, they are experiencing much more than aesthetic enjoyment or cultural voyeurism.

They feel, as I feel too because I've been so long acculturated to Zen, a religious feeling, a sense of connection to their ancestors, to the mystery of death and to the deep and saving truths that the Buddha taught, truths that lie at the heart of what it means to be Japanese.
And there is a great comfort in these experiences.
And this comfort is not, as Freud, the great scientist and the inventor of psychology as we know it, might have thought, the comfort that illusion brings.*

*It's the comfort of a palpable sense of shared, deep meaning, a feeling that you feel that's very direct, that one's busy and possibly frustrating and bewildering life has purpose and context, however undefined and even inexpressible that purpose and context may be.
In fact, this need for the validation of a sacred world on which a feeling of real meaning in one's life can be grounded, I think, is a basic human need.
And without it, individuals and whole societies go awry.*

*Another scene from Japan in July, very hot, Cathy and I were in Toji, which is I think the oldest Buddhist temple in Kyoto and possibly one of the oldest in all of Japan, this big compound that was full of the faithful who were crowding into the small shrine areas where memorial rituals were in progress.
It was the monthly memorial of Kobo Daishi, the founder of Toji.
People stood with palms together, some of them with tears in their eyes, overcome with memory or grief.*
*When the priests filed out of the shrine rooms, everyone bowed low with genuine respect.
It was beautiful.
We walked outside, and there standing by the entry gate, we saw a Buddhist nun shaking a Vajra implement with rings around it, making a jangling sound.
She was about 60 years old, and she looked like she'd been through a lot, but at the same time really serene and happy.
And as she played her little Vajra, she closed her eyes, and you could feel her body lifting up with the concentration of her standing meditation, and she began chanting sutras.
And as she was doing this, a really old woman walked by, bent over in half.
There's a lot of old people in Japan that you see bent over in half, I guess because of no milk in the early days of the 20th century.
It's not unusual to see a person like that.
And so this was an old woman walking by, and she bowed to the nun.*
*And the nun immediately broke off her concentration and smiled at the woman, and they began to talk.
And I can't understand Japanese.

They were standing actually right next to us as we were walking out, and I can't understand Japanese, but it seemed pretty clear that the old woman was telling the nun her troubles, was telling her all of her problems and sufferings.
And the nun was just standing there on the street listening, very sympathetically it seemed to the woman's story.
After the woman was finished, the nun then chanted some blessings for her, turned her around, and gave her a really good, brief but very good back massage.
The nun seemed to know what she was doing, how to give a good back massage.
Then turned her around again and jangled the Vajra and made some more blessings on her.
And the woman took some money out of her purse and put it in the alms bag of the nun and went on her way.*
*When we got home from Japan, and I became interested in Japan on the way home, that's when I read the guidebook.
It was a long flight.
I read the guidebook on the way home.
And of course the first thing we did is go and get a whole bunch of Japanese movies to watch.
So we watched a movie called—by Kenji Mizoguchi, a really classic Japanese film from the 50s—Ugetsu.
And in the plot of Ugetsu, ghosts figure prominently, which is not unusual.
Almost all traditional Japanese religion and storytelling includes this strong theme of two worlds.*
*One world is the tragic and yet quite ordinary world of daily living, a family of history.
It's a world in which people are constantly being victimized by their own passions or by social forces beyond their control.
The other world is a world of mystery, of death, ghosts, darkness and night.
This liminal world is also the world of the Buddha, a world that will be peaceful and free of trouble once the Buddha enters and subdues the dark side.
Though the liminal world is not part of the everyday, it bleeds into the everyday from time to time when you least expect it, so you can't ignore it.*
*And it is far larger and far more mysterious.
It's literally unknowable compared to the everyday world, and it's much more powerful.
The figure of the monastic in Japanese literature, as in the movie Ugetsu, is always representative of this mysterious world.
Whenever the monastic appears, you know that the liminal world is close at hand.
And the monastic's life of religious observance is for the purpose of staying in touch with this liminal world and as much as possible making sure that it remains benevolent.
In America, Zen is a religion of choice for a few adventuresome souls*
willing to invest themselves in something completely different.
Most serious American Zen practitioners are lay people who live ordinary lives in the world.
A minority become priests, but it doesn't do them much good because there is no social role in America for Zen priests.

Nor, as my friends who are priests can tell you, is there any reasonable way to earn a living through one's activity in that profession, which is probably why there aren't too many Zen priests in America.
In Japan, by contrast, almost all serious practitioners of Zen meditation are priests.
Being a priest in Japan is, as they used to say about 18th-century English parsons, a living.
Being a priest is a living in Japan.
And not only is it a living, it's a hereditary living.
The typical Japanese Zen priest is ordained by his father and expects to inherit his father's temple.
Our lineage here at Bellingham is the Soto Zen lineage.
Soto is the larger of the two main Japanese Zen sects.
In Japan, all Soto Zen priests are trained at one of two large monasteries: Eiheiji, located in the mountains of Echizen province, and Sojiji on the Noto Peninsula in Chugu.
Cathy and I made a visit to Eiheiji, the big training monastery, where Hoitsu Suzuki, an old dear friend and teacher of ours, is now serving, astonishingly enough to us, as Tanto, head of training.
So we went to visit, and he's a wonderful, wonderful man.
Very funny and impish and silly and great, but a bit forgetful.
So we arrived at Eiheiji's international section without the arrangements that Hoitsu promised he would make for us.
We just showed up and they said, oh, you're here.
However, it turned out that this was not a problem, because Kuro Yanagisan, the international director, knew my name, and he was very welcoming and immediately rolled out the red carpet.
We were given a very fancy formal tatami room with fold-out futons.
We were fed soon after we arrived with a sumptuous formal vegetarian meal, the like of which you cannot see anywhere on this continent.
This was all served to us by a young priest named Domyo, a very thin, young fellow who seemed enormously nervous at the prospect of taking care of an American Zen abbot in English.
This was really making him nervous.
He was called our assistant.

Actually, he was our keeper, because he told us in a very polite way, as he read from the instructions that he was supposed to read in English that was hard to understand, "Do not leave your room unless you are with me."
So although he was our assistant, he was also kind of like our keeper.
We were sort of in jail.
The next morning we got up really early, I think like 3 o'clock or something like that.
We did zazen, and then we attended the incredibly elaborate morning service of Eiheiji, which is held in the great Dharma hall.
This hall features a really large gold Buddha image, which is enshrined at one end of the room, high, high up on an altar that you can only reach by a set of very steep, long stairs.
The Buddha figure is enclosed behind screens that are opened up only for the service.
But even though the screens are opened up, the Buddha seems to be very far away and very distant and dark, mysterious.

There are two giant urns on either side of this altar, maybe 10 feet tall, full of lacquered, wooden, golden lotus flowers, in scale with the 10-foot urn, and lotus leaves and lotus seed pods, one urn on each side.
Hanging from the hall's heavy, wooden, beamed ceiling are four ornaments, also wooden, lacquered gold.
Two of them are really long and narrow.
They may be 20 feet long, hanging down 20 feet from the ceiling, maybe 5 feet wide, full of little filigrees and little bells and things.
The other two are like chandeliers, not as long, but wider, and these have even more elaborate bells and filigrees and parasols and banners and all kinds of things.
So the hall has a very high ceiling.
It feels very spacious.
And into the hall file the 220 or so training monks and the 30 or so officials who take care of them.
After they were all in the hall, Hoitsu arrived, because he was the officiant that morning, and he approached the really huge incense pot that stood before the altar.
The incense pot was so high that his attendant monk had to stand on tiptoes to get the stick of incense into the pot.
It so happened that it was the 15th of the month, so there was a special service, well over an hour of Japanese chanting.
The most spectacular part of the service was the passing out of sutra books by acolytes, who functioned as precisely and delicately as ballet dancers.
Absolutely.
You would have been astonished to see them.
They came in taking very careful, rhythmic, delicate sliding steps in their white-clad feet, holding a tray full of sutra books.
They would swivel around to each monastic with the tray, swooping down precisely in front of them.
The monastic would take the sutra book.

They would come up dramatically, swivel around to the next person and repeat this over and over down the line until they came to the end, at which point they would, with a flourish, turn around and go up to the next aisle, absolutely in tandem on either side of the hall.
It was quite something to see.
So you guys at Bellingham Zen Hall, take note of this.

What they were handing out was memorial names of temple donors, names that the faithful had paid to be chanted, some of them every day, some of them once a week, some of them once a month, some of them once a year, lots and lots and lots of names.
I don't know how many thousands of names.
The way they did that is every monk had his own list of names, and they all chanted at the same time different names.
So it made a very pleasant and odd, mumbly kind of cacophony as they did this.

There was also a food offering in the service, one of the attendants, in a very specific sideways fashion, climbing up the steep steps of the altar to offer the food, having to dodge behind these two gigantic lanterns, which also were about 10 or 12 feet tall, that were lighting the altar up.
And all this, with everything that was done, was done with an absolute precision and a gorgeous choreography.
So this is the training of an Eiheiji priest: ritual deportment.

These young men, and of course they're all men, are learning how to occupy the archetypal role of mediator between the worlds, how to deliver to parishioners the feeling of meaning, of protection, of peace, of comfort, that they expect and need from Buddhism.

So in addition to the garden, the art, the architecture, there is living ritual and the living presence of people who, however unschooled they may appear to be in meditative insight or religious text, in fact have been well trained to carry the feeling of Buddhism.
As we were leaving Eiheiji, Kuro Yanagi-san and I discussed this training and its effectiveness.
Like many other lively young Japanese Soto Zen priests, he was somewhat embarrassed by the formality and traditionalism of Eiheiji.
I guess maybe partly because he knew about my reputation of not being much that way, so maybe that contributed to his embarrassment.
He imagined that Americans by comparison are so rough and ready, so raw and real, that he was kind of embarrassed to see this kind of highly refined training.
And what did I think of it?
I said to him, "You know, we're doing the same thing.
We're trying our best to understand Buddhism and to offer it to people in whatever way that we can, for whatever good it might do them."

Despite this, and I think that's true, despite the truth of that, when I got home from Japan I reflected that Buddhism's meaning and cultural import in Japan and America are almost mirror opposites of one another.
In Japan, Buddhism was essential to the national character.
Literally, to be Japanese was to be Buddhist, no matter what your religion was.
And this historically is true.
What we know and call Japanese culture began with the Japanese people adopting Buddhism and using it as a centerpiece for their sense of being a people.
Therefore it's no wonder that the Japanese Buddhist establishment throughout the ages has been a staunch supporter always of the state, even in times of war and militarism, as I said before.
By contrast, in America, Buddhism seems to be for the outsider.
To be Buddhist in America is to take on a set of views and characteristics almost exactly opposed to the American spirit of rugged individualism and can-do materialism.
And another thing I thought about: like Japan, all the old cultures in the world have religion at their root.
We're a new culture, and we were founded on the opposite premise.
No established religion is fundamental to the founding of our nation.
This seems to us such an obvious requirement of freedom, democracy, and modernity that we don't even question it.
We all, I think, understand the many advantages of no established religion, things like fairness, inclusion, social and economic openness.
But we don't understand the disadvantages.
Without an established religion in our history, our culture has no taproot.
It has no unifying feeling or ritual.
No underlying sense of a shared reality that's wider than the material world.
So our culture has no coherent connection to the liminal world.
In place of this, we have our deified abstractions, freedom and democracy, about which we are even less clear than the Japanese are about Buddhism.
In America, we have no religious root that we can assume and rely on, deep in our bones.
The Japanese assume and rely on Buddhism.
The Russians, amazingly, despite 75 years of godless communism, still have the Orthodox Church in their bones.
And the Italians have the Roman Church, and so on and so on.
Almost all old cultures have this.
Because of this cultural lack, American religions tend to fall into one of two extremes.

Either they become an enthusiastic and totalizing ideology, as if to compensate for their shallow rootedness, or, deeply influenced by the fact that being too religiously identified is un-American, they become so domesticated and damped down that they lose all their healing and saving power.
Probably no country in the world has this paradoxical relationship to religion.
We are at once the most secular and the most hysterically religious nation on earth.
And it may be that these two opposite things depend on each other.
We are hysterically religious in reaction to our ingrained secularism, and we are fiercely secular as an antidote to our religious lunacy.

Now, if this dialectic between the secular and the religious threatens to tear up our society, because the red and the blue states are coexisting now in a state of dormant, quiet, but yet potent hostility, how much more so is it also tearing up our world?
During the medieval period, Islam evolved into the most broad-minded and tolerant religion the world had ever known.
But during the 20th century, it began to respond to Western colonial secularism with hysterical forms that have by now succeeded in capturing the world's attention, if not entirely obsessing it.
So I've been thinking about these things a lot since September 11, 2001.
To me, it seems really obvious that when we say globalism, globalization of the planet, what we're really talking about is the Americanization of the planet.
This is so completely and obviously the case that I think we as Americans don't notice it.
We don't think of globalization as Americanization.
It's simply the sharing of modern ideas and tools, things that anyone would want, right?
How is this not a good thing?
Who could doubt that freedom, democracy, and the secularism that seems to inevitably go along with modernity are universal benefits that everyone should share in?
Who doubts this?
The global world will be a world of exciting free markets that will proliferate goods and the desire for goods and will bring people together in a congregation of universal consumerism.
Now, we all know, nobody would deny, that materialism can go too far.

But this is not to be worried about, because in the modern, postmodern world there's freedom, and people are free to choose whatever religious persuasion they're interested in, and the marketplace will allow that.
The only thing is that this religion is a private, personal matter, and it has no place in public.
The only public forum that matters and that we can discuss things in is the marketplace.
Now, most of us feel pretty comfortable with this, actually, and it suits us well because this is our historical context.
But it's possible that for other people in other parts of the world, private religion that occupies no social or political space is not satisfying.

A worldview that rejects the bewildering roller coaster ride that postmodern society has become, a really wild ride that has no respect for or even any acknowledgement of the liminal world that has always, always up to now been a part of any society, that worldview may not be entirely negative.
There may be deeper and more historically potent reasons than we have imagined for the rise of Islamic fundamentalism and for the rise of religious fanaticism in our own culture.
These phenomena may not be so easily dismissed as, in the one case, evil and, in the other, stupid.
It may be that there is something here we ought to pay attention to, something here we ought to be seriously engaged with rather than something that we need to flee from and dismiss.

Is it possible that, like a tantrum-prone child full of powerful feelings she's unable to express in an adult conversation whose terms seem necessarily opaque, Islamic and other religious fundamentalisms are humanity's desperate attempt to break through again to the liminal world we thought we could leave behind?
If that were so, we would then need something much more than a war on terror or a domestic political strategy to defeat the quote-unquote religious right.
We may need to take stock at a deeper level, yes, even at a religious level, of who and what we have become.
So what would that stock-taking look like?
Well, that's probably another essay, but I'll end with a few thoughts.
First, maybe we need to consider the possibility that fundamentalists are correct in their belief that religion needs to be more than private and personal.
Maybe it does need to be a basis of our shared social life in a way that we haven't thought of.
Suppose that were so.
What would that possibly mean in a world that is so incredibly multicultural now that it is not all that unusual in a single nuclear family for there to be two or three religions?
How would you create social space for religion in that case?
I think it would mean an approach to religion that references the human heart as much as, or more than it references, God, doctrine, or belief of whatever stripe.
I think it would also mean new forms of religious practice, including practices that could be shared by people of different faiths.
It would certainly mean a new understanding of the place and meaning of religious practice in our society and in our personal lives.

And most of all, it would mean that we would have to learn to do something that we have never been able to do, but that we have always desperately needed to do: to talk to one another, peacefully, about the things that matter to us most.
So that's my essay for the Sun.
I don't know how much of that will appear in the Sun, because they usually have a big red pencil and they say this is dominant.
So you never know.
I've gotten used to that over the years.
I write it and then it's theirs.
Whatever you want to do with it, go ahead.

verbatim.text: Well, as Tim said, I've been a full-time Zen student for a long time. Actually, my entire adult life, and this has been a big surprise to me. This was not my intention. I began as an artist, a poet, and I still maintain my poetry practice after all this time. But I realized early on in my career as a poet that what interested me was not recording or expressing my life. And I wasn't all that terribly impressed by beautiful and eloquent words. I realized that I just had questions about reality.

And somehow it seemed to me that poetry would be one way of exploring these questions. And these were the same questions that eventually led me to study Zen, and to keep studying Zen until today. So despite myself, I have become interested in religion. I'm interested in this. What is religion, actually? Why is it that everywhere in the world you find people practicing different religions? Why is it that when you go back and dig up the ruins of some super ancient city, you find that they practice religion in every culture known to humankind?

Why is it that religion always goes wrong somehow? Why is this the most common thing in the world? What does religion have to do with our psychological lives? What does religion have to do with our social lives? And it just turned out that since I've been doing Zen practice for such a long time, and in this time when Zen is being transmitted for the first time to the West, I've had a chance to explore these questions. And my life, in a way, you could say, has been kind of living out of many of these questions.

And sometimes, because of my unfortunate writing habit, I end up writing about these questions. Not because I know the answers to them, but because I want to raise these questions out loud. So this summer I was on a trip to Japan, and that gave me another place from which to view my questions. When I came back from Japan, the editors of Sun magazine, you know that magazine, The Sun? Yeah. So I didn't really know the magazine much, but somehow I had written some article that they published, and they emailed me and they said, would you write an article for The Sun? And I said, OK, what if I write an article about my trip to Japan and some thoughts that I have about that?

And they said, OK. So I sent them a copy of the article and they thought it would be a good idea to publish it. So what I want to do tonight is actually try out this draft of this article on you and see what you think. And you can tell me afterward if you think it makes any sense. And the title of the article is Zen and the Two Worlds. And it is a bit of a travelogue, and I hope that you'll have fun joining me in a trip to Japan. But also partly it's some reflections on these questions that I've mentioned. So here's the article. We were in Fuji-Kawaguchiko, a resort town on one of the large lakes at the foot of Mount Fuji in Japan.

It was July. We'd come to see and even possibly climb Mount Fuji, but of course we couldn't see Mount Fuji at all, only roiling silver-gray clouds which were attractive in their own way. We weren't disappointed. We'd expected as much. Japanese summers are famously humid, and so they're often also cloudy and rainy. And Fuji's absence is nearly as famous as its presence. Besides, I am used to the idea that the more you count on the arrival of a very important experience or accomplishment you are so much planning on, the more likely it is that it won't materialize. And that instead you might get to enjoy something completely different.

Studying such normal human phenomena is one of the pleasures of Zen practice. When I was avid of Gringolch Farms Zen Center in the country near San Francisco, we'd go out every year in the pre-dawn for the annual celebration of Buddha's enlightenment. The idea was that we were going out to see the morning star, just as the Buddha had seen the morning star on the night of his awakening. Most years we saw fog, no stars. So I had been practicing this for many years, and so my wife Cathy and I were not too fazed by the fact that we were not, as the brochure promised,

sitting in the ofuro of our hotel gazing out at Mount Fuji. But instead we were strolling around Lake Kawaguchi under very active clouds. The path around the lake was bordered with tall grasses and extensive plantings of gorgeous blue, pink, purple, and white hydrangeas that were much more delicate and subtle than the big garish ones you see in old-fashioned American gardens. And though there were a fair number of resort hotels around the lake, the path this day was unpeopled. We shared the walk only with a backpacking European couple,

an old Japanese man walking his teensy white dog, and an ancient farmer tending his vegetable patch. Though a resort town, Fuji-Kawaguchiko, is not fancy or overdone, in fact, it's a rather ordinary, dull spot. And we spent a lot of time walking up and down the streets whose local shops reminded me of the small town I grew up in in the days before malls and high-concept chain stores made shopping exciting rather than utilitarian. Fuji-Kawaguchiko streets were a far cry from the glitz and glam

that we'd experienced in Kyoto's downtown precincts. One of our strolls we noticed, as one can notice almost anywhere in Japan, even on busy, wild streets, we noticed a torii gate that signaled the entrance to a small temple compound, so we went in. Walking into the temple compound was like walking literally into another universe, a place that was quiet, serene, and felt holy. Just beyond the gate was a small mossy garden with irregular stepping stones that led to a steadily dripping, tiny, delicate waterfall.

Off to one side was a standing figure of Guanyin, Bodhisattva of Compassion, on a formal lotus pedestal, looking down at us with a modest and knowing smile that carried the ancient Buddhist feeling that all would be well in the midst of a world of inevitable suffering. The temple building, like the garden, was solid. It was really beautiful. It was well-kept. And though its heavy wooden door was locked, you could walk around on the veranda or you could sit on the steps looking out into the garden.

We felt really at home here. Everything slowed down. We were refreshed. For years I've been impatient with Japanese Buddhism's formality, aestheticism, and basic irrelevance to any sort of actual spiritual transformation. When I began studying Zen in 1970 and reading about it some years before that, my attitude was almost the reverse of this. In those days I was really enamored of Japanese Zen's dynamic relationship to the arts. And I don't think I would be exaggerating to say that in Japan all the traditional arts owe their existence to Zen.

And I loved the Japanese sensibility in general and Zen's relationship to it. And that's what appealed to me. It was a long time ago. I was young. I was a poet. I was part of a generation that was in revolt against American values. And everything Japanese struck me as entirely superior in every way to the crude violence of the West. But that was 1970. All my years of Zen practice in America had changed my attitude drastically.

Seeing the raw and actual spiritual needs of people I was practicing with, I came to realize that flower arranging, tea sipping, and raked gravel gardening was not going to be of much help to them. And certainly the complicated, bureaucratic, and stiflingly traditional Japanese Zen establishment that I'd come to know and have dealings with over the years was probably also not going to help them. Meditation practice might help. Teachings about how to work with suffering, with afflictive states of mind, might help.

Communities of support and guidance might help. But I don't think flower arranging would help. So between Japanese Zen's general irrelevance and also the new scholarship that was just since I guess the late 80s, early 90s, the new scholarship that was just being done that was highlighting Japanese Zen's really shameful conduct during the period before and during World War II. With all this, I had gradually, without even necessarily realizing it, developed a fairly thoroughgoing antipathy toward Japanese Zen.

And this is rather an odd and troubling attitude for a senior American Zen priest and abbot in a Japanese lineage to have. So I didn't particularly consider this a problem or even notice it or pay any attention to it until when we were getting ready to go to Japan. By the way, it was my wife Cathy's idea to go to Japan, not my idea. I was going because she wanted to go. I'd been to Japan before and I had no intention of ever going back. But she wanted to go, so I went.

Anyway, preparing for the trip to Japan, we went into the Japanese tourist office in San Francisco because we needed to get a Japan Rail Pass and you have to go to the Japanese tourist office to get that. And as soon as I walked into that obscure sort of 10th floor office in a downtown building in San Francisco, it was like going to Japan. Just walking into the Japanese tourist office, it was like going to Japan. The place was very quiet, stacked all over with clutter like a typical Japanese office or home.

And everybody who works in the Japanese tourist office in San Francisco is Japanese, not Japanese American, but Japanese. So as soon as you enter the space, you feel the pervasive aura of politeness and quiet courtesy that really is at the heart of the Japanese way of being. It's possible that arrogance and aggression are also basic to the Japanese way of being. I don't know. But anyway, these things were not in evidence in the Japanese tourist office. Just to walk into the Japanese tourist office in San Francisco

and interact with the people there who were so wonderful and so sweet, it just melted my heart. And it reminded me of how tenderly I used to feel about all things Japanese and what a warm feeling I always had whenever I would encounter Japanese people. And I still have that feeling, actually, but I forgot about it. And so it kind of came out when I went to the tourist office. But you know, it occurred to me that this is what happens to every one of us. In the ordinary course of things, we fix on something that is partly true and partly not true.

And without realizing it, we fix that notion into a prejudice. And then prejudiced or blind to the other possibilities, unless we're lucky enough to go into the Japanese tourist office. So in a similar way, entering that small and quite ordinary temple compound in Fujikawa Guchiko reminded me that actually there is more to Japanese Zen than formality, bureaucracy, and aesthetics. We in the West have managed to take the quiet, holy, sacred world and reduce it to what we call the inner life, which can be safely crammed into the space between our ears.

Our scientific spirit has given us explanations that tame and disarm the uncharted world of mystery and allow us to dispense with the need for powers beyond ourselves. Japanese society, too, is saturated with the scientific spirit. But unlike ours, it has preserved in its atavistic layers a Buddhist religious sensibility. However unclear that sensibility may be to most Japanese people, it nevertheless lives within and all around them. When Japanese people enter a temple compound,

they are experiencing much more than aesthetic enjoyment or cultural voyeurism. They feel, as I feel too because I've been so long acculturated to Zen, a religious feeling, a sense of connection to their ancestors, to the mystery of death and to the deep and saving truths that the Buddha taught, truths that lie at the heart of what it means to be Japanese. And there is a great comfort in these experiences. And this comfort is not, as Freud, the great scientist and the inventor of psychology as we know it, this comfort is not, as Freud might have thought, the comfort that illusion brings.

It's the comfort of a palpable sense of shared, deep meaning, a feeling that you feel that's very direct, that one's busy and possibly frustrating and bewildering life has purpose and context, however undefined and even inexpressible that purpose and context may be. In fact, this need for the validation of a sacred world on which a feeling of real meaning in one's life can be grounded, I think, is a basic human need. And without it, individuals and whole societies go awry.

Another scene from Japan in July, very hot, Cathy and I were in Toji, which is I think the oldest Buddhist temple in Kyoto and possibly one of the oldest in all of Japan, this big compound that was full of the faithful who were crowding into the small shrine areas where memorial rituals were in progress. It was the monthly memorial of Kobo Daishi, the founder of Toji. People stood with palms together, some of them with tears in their eyes, overcome with memory or grief.

When the priests filed out of the shrine rooms, everyone bowed low with genuine respect. It was beautiful. We walked outside, and there standing by the entry gate, we saw a Buddhist nun shaking a Vajra implement with rings around it, making a jangling sound. She was about 60 years old, and she looked like she'd been through a lot, but at the same time really serene and happy.

And as she played her little Vajra, she closed her eyes, and you could feel her body lifting up with the concentration of her standing meditation, and she began chanting sutras. And as she was doing this, a really old woman walked by, bent over in half. There's a lot of old people in Japan that you see bent over in half, I guess because of no milk in the early days of the 20th century. It's not unusual to see a person like that. And so this was an old woman walking by, and she bowed to the nun.

And the nun immediately broke off her concentration and smiled at the woman, and they began to talk. And I can't understand Japanese. They were standing actually right next to us as we were walking out, and I can't understand Japanese, but it seemed pretty clear that the old woman was telling the nun her troubles, was telling her all of her problems and sufferings. And the nun was just standing there on the street listening,

very sympathetically it seemed to the woman's story. After the woman was finished, the nun then chanted some blessings for her, turned her around, and gave her a really good, brief but very good back massage. The nun seemed to know what she was doing, how to give a good back massage. Then turned her around again and jangled the Vajra and made some more blessings on her. And the woman took some money out of her purse and put it in the alms bag of the nun and went on her way. When we got home from Japan, and I became interested in Japan on the way home,

that's when I read the guidebook. It was a long flight. I read the guidebook on the way home. And of course the first thing we did is go and get a whole bunch of Japanese movies to watch. So we watched a movie called, by Kenji Mizoguchi, a really classic Japanese film from the 50s called Ugetsu. And in the plot of Ugetsu, ghosts figure prominently, which is not unusual. Almost all traditional Japanese religion and storytelling includes this strong theme of two worlds.

One world is the tragic and yet quite ordinary world of daily living, a family of history. It's a world in which people are constantly being victimized by their own passions or by social forces beyond their control. The other world is a world of mystery, of death, ghosts, darkness and night. This liminal world is also the world of the Buddha, a world that will be peaceful and free of trouble once the Buddha enters and subdues the dark side. Though the liminal world is not part of the everyday, it bleeds into the everyday from time to time when you least expect it, so you can't ignore it.

And it is far larger and far more mysterious. It's literally unknowable compared to the everyday world, and it's much more powerful. The figure of the monastic in Japanese literature, as in the movie Ugetsu, is always representative of this mysterious world. Whenever the monastic appears, you know that the liminal world is close at hand. And the monastic's life of religious observance is for the purpose of staying in touch with this liminal world and as much as possible making sure that it remains benevolent. In America, Zen is a religion of choice for a few adventuresome souls

willing to invest themselves in something completely different. Most serious American Zen practitioners are lay people who live ordinary lives in the world. A minority become priests, but it doesn't do them much good because there is no social role in America for Zen priests, nor, as my friends who are priests can tell you, there is no reasonable way to earn a living through one's activity in that profession, which is probably why there aren't too many Zen priests in America. In Japan, by contrast, almost all serious practitioners of Zen meditation are priests. Being a priest in Japan is, as they used to say about 18th century English Parsons,

being a priest is a living in Japan. And not only is it a living, it's a hereditary living. The typical Japanese Zen priest is ordained by his father and expects and will inherit his father's temple. Our lineage here at Bellingham is the Soto Zen lineage. Soto is the largest of the two, larger of the two main Japanese Zen sects. And in Japan, all Soto Zen priests are trained at one of two large monasteries, Eiheiji, located in the mountains of Echizen province in Sojiji on the Noto Peninsula in Chugu. And Cathy and I made a visit to Eiheiji, the big training monastery, where Hoitsu Suzuki, who's an old dear friend and teacher of ours,

astonishingly enough to us, is serving now as Tanto, head of training. So we went to visit, and he's a wonderful, wonderful man. Very funny and impish and silly and great, but a bit forgetful. So we arrived at Eiheiji's international section without the arrangements that Hoitsu promised he would make for us. We just showed up and they said, oh, you're here. However, it turned out that this was not a problem because Kuro Yanagisan, the international director, knew my name and he was very welcoming and immediately rolled out the red carpet. And we were given a very fancy formal tatami room with fold-out futons.

And we were fed soon after we arrived with a sumptuous formal vegetarian meal, the like of which you cannot see anywhere on this continent. And this was all served to us by a young priest named Domyo, a very thin, young fellow who seemed enormously nervous at the prospect of taking care of an American Zen abbot in English. This was really making him nervous. He was called our assistant. Actually, he was our keeper because he told us in a very polite way,

as he read from the instructions that he was supposed to read in English that was hard to understand. He basically said to us, do not leave your room unless you are with me. So although he was our assistant, he was also kind of like our keeper. And we were sort of in jail. The next morning, so we went to bed. The next morning we got up early, really early, I think like 3 o'clock or something like that. And we did zazen and then we attended the incredibly elaborate morning service of a heiji, which is held in the great Dharma hall.

This hall features a large, really large gold Buddha image, which is enshrined at one end of the room. High, high up on an altar that you can only reach by a set of very steep, long stairs. And the Buddha figure is enclosed behind screens that are opened up only for the service. But even though the screens are opened up, the Buddha seems to be very far away and very distant and dark, mysterious. There are two giant urns on either side of this altar, about maybe 10 feet tall, full of flowers, lacquered, wooden, golden lacquered flowers that are lotus flowers, in scale with this 10-foot urn, and lotus leaves, lotus flowers, and lotus seed pods, one on each side.

Hanging from the hall's heavy, wooden, beamed ceiling are four ornaments, also wooden, lacquered gold. Two of them are really long and narrow. They may be 20 feet long, hanging down 20 feet from the ceiling, maybe 5 feet wide, full of little filigrees and little bells and things. And the other two are like chandeliers, not as long, but wider. And these have even more elaborate bells and filigrees and parasols and banners and all kinds of things. So the hall has a very high ceiling. It feels very spacious. And into the hall file the 220 or so training monks and the 30 or so officials who take care of them.

After they were all in the hall, Hoitsu arrived, because he was the officiant that morning, and he approached the really huge incense pot that then stood before the altar. And the pot, incense pot, was so high that his attendant monk had to stand on tiptoes to get the stick of incense into the pot. It so happened that it was the 15th of the month, so there was a special service, well over an hour of Japanese chanting. The most spectacular part of the service was the passing out of sutra books by acolytes, who functioned as precisely and delicately as ballet dancers. Absolutely. You would have been astonished to see them.

They came in taking very careful, rhythmic, delicate sliding steps in their white-clad feet, holding a tray full of sutra books. They would swivel around to each monastic with the tray, swooped down precisely in front of them. The monastic would take the sutra book. They would come up dramatically, swivel around to the next person and repeat this over and over down the line until they came to the end, at which point they would, with a flourish, turn around and go up to the next aisle, absolutely in tandem on either side of the hall. It was quite something to see. So you guys at Bellingham Zen Hall, take note of this. What they were handing out was memorial names of temple donors,

names that the faithful had paid to be chanted, some of them every day, some of them once a week, some of them once a month, some of them once a year, lots and lots and lots of names. I don't know how many thousands of names. And the way they did that is they would, every monk had his own list of names and they all chanted at the same time different names. So it made a very pleasant and odd, mumbly kind of cacophony as they did this. There was also a food offering in the service, one of the attendants, in a very specific sideways fashion, climbing up the steep steps of the altar to offer the food, having to dodge behind these two gigantic lanterns, which also were about 10 or 12 feet tall,

that were lighting the altar up. And all this, with everything that was done, was done with an absolute precision and a gorgeous choreography. So this is the training of an Heiji priest, ritual deportment. These young men, and of course they're all men, are learning how to occupy the archetypal role of mediator between the worlds, how to deliver to parishioners the feeling of meaning, of protection, of peace, of comfort, that they expect and need from Buddhism. So in addition to the garden, the art, the architecture, there is living ritual

and the living presence of people who, however unschooled they may appear to be, in meditative insight or religious text, in fact have been well trained to carry the feeling of Buddhism. As we were leaving Heiji, Kuro Yanagi-san and I discussed this training and its effectiveness. Like many other lively young Japanese Soto Zen priests, he was somewhat embarrassed by the formality and traditionalism of Heiji. I guess maybe partly because he knew about my reputation of not being much that way, so maybe that contributed to his embarrassment. And he imagined that Americans by comparison are so rough and ready, so raw and real,

that he was kind of embarrassed to see this kind of highly refined training. And what did I think of it? But I said to him, you know, we're doing the same thing. We're trying our best to understand Buddhism and to offer it to people in whatever way that we can, for whatever good it might do them. Despite this, and I think that's true, despite the truth of that, when I got home from Japan I reflected that Buddhism's meaning and cultural import in Japan and America are almost mirror opposites of one another.

In Japan, Buddhism was essential to the national character. Literally, to be Japanese was to be Buddhist, no matter what your religion was. And this historically is true. What we know and call Japanese culture began with the Japanese people adopting Buddhism and using it as a centerpiece for their sense of being a people. And therefore it's no wonder that the Japanese Buddhist establishment throughout the ages has been a staunch supporter always of the state, even in times of war and militarism, as I said before.

By contrast, in America, Buddhism seems to be for the outsider. To be Buddhist in America is to take on a set of views and characteristics almost exactly opposed to the American spirit of rugged individualism and can-do materialism. And another thing I thought about. Like Japan, all the old cultures in the world have religion at their root. We're a new culture and we were founded on the opposite premise. No established religion that's fundamental to the founding of our nation. And this seems to us such an obvious requirement of freedom, democracy, and modernity

that we don't even question it. We all, I think, understand the many advantages of no established religion. Things like fairness, inclusion, social and economic openness. But we don't understand the disadvantages. Without an established religion in our history, our culture has no taproot. It has no unifying feeling or ritual. No underlying sense of a shared reality that's wider than the material world. So our culture has no coherent connection to the liminal world.

In place of this, we have our deified abstractions. Freedom and democracy, about which we are even less clear than the Japanese are about Buddhism. In America, we have no religious root that we can assume and rely on, deep in our bones. The Japanese assume and rely on Buddhism. The Russians, amazingly, despite 75 years of godless communism, still have the Orthodox Church in their bones. And the Italians have the Roman Church, and so on and so on.

Almost all old cultures have this. Because of this cultural lack, American religions tend to fall into one of two extremes. Either they become an enthusiastic and totalizing ideology, as if to compensate for their shallow rootedness, or deeply influenced by the fact that being too religiously identified is un-American. They become so domesticated and damped down that they lose all their healing and saving power. Probably no country in the world has this paradoxical relationship to religion. We are at once the most secular and the most hysterically religious nation on earth.

And it may be that these two opposite things depend on each other. We are hysterically religious in reaction to our ingrained secularism. And we are fiercely secular as an antidote to our religious lunacy. Now, if this dialectic between the secular and the religious threatens to tear up our society, because the red and the blue states are coexisting now in a state of dormant, quiet, but yet potent hostility, how much more so is it also tearing up our world? During the medieval period, Islam evolved into the most broad-minded and tolerant religion the world had ever known. But during the 20th century, it began to respond to Western colonial secularism with hysterical forms

that have by now succeeded in capturing the world's attention, if not entirely obsessing it. So, I've been thinking about these things a lot since September 11, 2001. To me, it seems really obvious that when we say globalism, globalization of the planet, what we're really talking about is the Americanization of the planet. And this is so completely and obviously the case that I think we as Americans don't notice it. We don't think of globalization as Americanization. It's simply the sharing of modern ideas and tools, things that anyone would want, right? How is this not a good thing?

Who could doubt that freedom, democracy, and the secularism that seems to inevitably go along with modernity are universal benefits that everyone should share in? Who doubts this? The global world will be a world of exciting free markets that will proliferate goods and the desire for goods and will bring people together in a congregation of universal consumerism. Now, we all know, nobody would deny, that materialism can go too far. But this is not to be worried about because in the modern, postmodern world, there's freedom and people are free to choose whatever religious persuasion that they're interested in

and the marketplace will allow that. The only thing is that this religion is a private, personal matter and it has no place in public. The only public forum that matters and that we can discuss things in is the marketplace. Now, most of us feel pretty comfortable with this, actually, and it suits us well because this is our historical context. But it's possible that for other people in other parts of the world, private religion that occupies no social or political space is not satisfying. A worldview that rejects the bewildering roller coaster ride that postmodern society has become,

a really wild ride that has no respect for or even any acknowledgement of the liminal world that has always, always up to now been a part of any society, that worldview may not be entirely negative. There may be deeper and more historically potent reasons than we have imagined for the rise of Islamic fundamentalism and for the rise of religious fanaticism in our own culture. These phenomena may not be so easily dismissed as, on the one case, evil and on the other, stupid. It may be that there is something here we ought to pay attention to, something here we ought to be seriously engaged with rather than something that we need to flee from and dismiss. Is it possible that, like a tantrum-prone child full of powerful feelings,

she's unable to express, in an adult conversation whose terms seem necessarily opaque, that Islamic and other religious fundamentalisms are humanity's desperate attempt to break through again to the liminal world we thought we could leave behind? If that were so, we would then need something much more than a war on terror or a domestic political strategy to defeat the quote-unquote religious right. We may need to take stock at a deeper level, yes, even at a religious level, of who and what we have become. So what would that stock-taking look like? Well, that's probably another essay, but I'll end with a few thoughts.

First, maybe we need to consider the possibility that fundamentalists are correct in their belief that religion needs to be more than private and personal. Maybe it does need to be a basis of our shared social life in a way that we haven't thought of. Suppose that were so. What would that possibly mean in a world that is so incredibly multicultural now that it is not all that unusual in a single nuclear family for there to be two or three religions? How would you create social space for religion in that case? I think it would mean an approach to religion that references the human heart

as much as, or more than it references, God, doctrine, or belief of whatever stripe. I think it would also mean new forms of religious practice, including practices that could be shared by people of different faiths. And it would certainly mean a new understanding of the place and meaning of religious practice in our society and in our personal lives. And most of all, it would mean that we would have to learn to do something that we have never been able to do, but that we have always desperately needed to do. To talk to one another, peacefully, about the things that matter to us most.

So that's my essay for the sun. I don't know how much of that will appear in the sun, because they usually have a big red pencil and they say this is dominant. So you never know. I've gotten used to that over the years. I write it and then it's theirs. Whatever you want to do with it, go ahead.
